title: Requesting Records on Opioid Settlement Spending
text: Public records laws allow journalists and members of the public to request documents from government agencies, including their documentation of opioid settlement funds received and how they’re spending them.

title: Requesting Records on Opioid Settlement Spending
text:
Understanding open records laws
At the federal level, these laws fall under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA). However, most records related to opioid settlement spending are held by state and local governments, which operate under state-level open records laws.
These laws vary widely across states. Some states have strong transparency protections, clear deadlines, and limited exemptions. Others have weaker laws, slower response timelines, or broader exemptions.
To learn the specific rules in your state, consult:

Investigative Reporters and Editors (IRE) FOIA resources
State press association open records guides
Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press open government guide

Understanding your state’s law will help you determine:

How long agencies have to respond
What fees, if any, they can charge
What exemptions they may claim
Whether you can appeal a denial

title: Requesting Records on Opioid Settlement Spending
text:
What to request
Investigating opioid settlement spending begins with requesting documents that show both how much funding governments have received and how decisions about spending are made.
Municipal and county governments often hold many of the most important records, including:

Budget documents
Contracts with treatment providers
Grant applications
Meeting minutes
Financial ledgers
Checks or payment records
Emails discussing allocations

title: Requesting Records on Opioid Settlement Spending
text:
Using MuckRock
MuckRock is a platform that simplifies filing, tracking, and publishing public records requests. During the West Virginia investigation, the MuckRock support team helped:

Locate or verify agency contact information
Add counties or offices not already listed in the system
Troubleshoot delivery or submission issues
Update request routing when agencies redirected requests to another office
Provide guidance on how to proceed when agencies stopped responding

MuckRock staff may also suggest alternative agency contacts, different submission methods, or ways to revise or narrow requests to improve response rates.






Tip



For large collaborative investigations involving many jurisdictions, MuckRock’s support can help reporters maintain consistency and avoid delays caused by incorrect contact information or administrative issues.

title: Requesting Records on Opioid Settlement Spending
text:
When agencies fail to respond
Tracking follow-ups is especially important when requesting records from multiple jurisdictions. During the West Virginia investigation, several counties only responded after repeated follow-up emails or phone calls.
If an agency doesn’t respond:

Send follow-up emails referencing the original request and submission date
Call the agency directly to confirm the request was received
Ask whether clarification or narrowing of the request is needed
Keep detailed notes of all communication attempts and response dates

In some cases, delays or refusals to provide records may themselves become part of the reporting — particularly when agencies overseeing significant public funding provide limited transparency.






Note



Some counties refused to use MuckRock and instead required requests to be submitted through direct email or standard mail. If this happens, requests can still be tracked and published through MuckRock even if communication occurs outside the platform.

title: Requesting Records on Opioid Settlement Spending
text:
Common problems
Although opioid settlement records are considered public documents, accessing them is not always straightforward. During the months of the West Virginia investigation, the records request process varied significantly from county to county.
One of the most common problems was simply receiving a response. Some counties:

Did not respond to requests at all
Required multiple follow-up emails and phone calls
Delayed responses beyond expected timelines
Redirected requests between offices or departments

In some cases, counties refused to use MuckRock. Other counties required reporters to:

Travel in person to review records
Pay fees for copies of documents
Review paper records instead of digital files
Pick up records physically rather than receive them electronically

Records were also purchased from several counties, including Kanawha County, Harrison County, and Hancock County.
Another challenge involved the records themselves. Public records responses rarely arrived in a consistent or organized format. Documents were often spread across multiple PDFs, scans, or paper files with little explanation or labeling. Many records were handwritten, scanned poorly, or incomplete — requiring significant cleanup and organization before analysis could begin.

title: What’s in the Data – and How to Get It
text: During the West Virginia investigation, a standardized public records request was sent to each county. Using consistent request language made it easier to compare responses across jurisdictions and organize records once they were received.

title: What’s in the Data – and How to Get It
text:
What to ask for
Request documents that show:

The total amount of opioid settlement funds received
How those funds were allocated or distributed
The process used to determine funding decisions
Which programs or organizations received settlement dollars

title: What’s in the Data – and How to Get It
text:
Sample request language
The following language can be adapted for most state or local open records laws:

Please provide any and all documents relating to the following:

The total amount of opioid settlement funds your office has received.
Documentation showing the distribution or allocation of opioid settlement funds.
Any guidelines, policies, or procedures used to evaluate requests for funding.
Documentation describing how applications for settlement funding are reviewed or approved.


Because recordkeeping practices vary widely, reporters may also need to request additional materials that provide context for how decisions are made:

Grant or funding applications submitted by organizations
Meeting minutes where settlement spending was discussed
Emails or correspondence between officials about allocations
Records showing which organizations received funding and how much

title: What’s in the Data – and How to Get It
text:
What you’ll receive
During the West Virginia investigation, public records responses arrived in many different formats:

Budget documents outlining settlement allocations
Physical ledgers
Receipt forms
Scanned financial ledgers and checks
Meeting minutes discussing settlement spending
Applications with local organizations
Project outlines

These records often arrived without standardized formatting and required significant organization before they could be analyzed.

title: What’s in the Data – and How to Get It
text:
Tracking requests across jurisdictions
When requesting records from multiple counties or cities, track requests in a spreadsheet documenting:

Submission dates
Response deadlines
Whether agencies fulfilled, denied, or delayed requests

This allows reporters to identify patterns in transparency and compare spending decisions across jurisdictions.
Because opioid settlement payments will continue for many years, these records provide an ongoing opportunity for journalists to monitor how funds are used and whether spending aligns with public health recommendations.

title: Strategies for Organizing and Sorting Documents
text:
Public records responses often arrive in many formats and can be difficult to interpret. During the West Virginia investigation, a wide range of materials were received, including scanned financial ledgers, individual checks, budget spreadsheets, meeting minutes, contracts and grant agreements, and emails between officials.
These records were rarely standardized and often required significant organization before analysis.

title: Strategies for Organizing and Sorting Documents
text:
Managing large document sets
To make sense of large document collections:

Create a central document storage system — the WV investigation used DocumentCloud
Label files consistently by jurisdiction and document type — DocumentCloud’s tags and key-value pairs feature makes this practical
Track where each document came from
Record key information in a spreadsheet or database

For each document, you may want to log:

Agency name
Amount of settlement funding received
Allocation decisions
Program descriptions
Date of spending approval

title: Strategies for Organizing and Sorting Documents
text:
Using DocumentCloud
DocumentCloud is a platform for uploading, organizing, annotating, and publishing primary source documents. The WV investigation used it as the central repository for all received records.
This process of uploading and tagging documents provides key data to journalists around the state and even the country. Reporting on county-level spending has been very small, and without this kind of organized document work some of this data could have been lost.
Many newspapers and news outlets do not have the resources, staff, or time to report on state, county, and city/municipality opioid settlement funding — making a well-organized DocumentCloud project a public resource beyond just your own reporting.

Tagging documents
A tag is a specific search key term added to individual documents to make it easier to search for specific information and keep all received documents organized by municipality, county, or city. When searching for a county’s specific documents, only those tagged with that county will appear.
To tag a document in DocumentCloud:

Upload the document
Click on it to open it
Select the tagging option
In the “new item” box, enter the category (e.g., county or city)
In the value box, enter the specific name (e.g., Kanawha County)



Key-value pairs
Beyond simple tags, DocumentCloud’s key-value pairs allow you to attach structured metadata to each document — useful for recording amounts, dates, and other data points you want to query later.

title: Strategies for Organizing and Sorting Documents
text:
Turning documents into data
Many investigative projects require converting unstructured documents into structured data. This process may involve:

Manually reviewing financial records
Extracting spending amounts
Categorizing spending by program type
Comparing spending patterns across jurisdictions

While time-consuming, this process allows reporters to identify patterns, inconsistencies, or unexpected spending decisions that would otherwise remain buried in individual PDFs.

title: Reporting Threads and Investigative Angles
text: Once records are collected and organized, several potential reporting angles may emerge. The following threads were developed during the West Virginia investigation and can be adapted for any jurisdiction.

title: Reporting Threads and Investigative Angles
text:
How funds are allocated
Investigate how local governments decide where settlement funds should go. Key questions include:

Who participates in spending decisions?
Are advisory boards involved?
Are decisions documented in public meetings?

In the West Virginia investigation, reporting examined how counties distributed settlement funds to local organizations and community initiatives, as well as how those decisions were approved.

title: Reporting Threads and Investigative Angles
text:
Evidence-based spending
Public health experts have identified several strategies supported by research, including treatment programs and harm reduction services. Reporting can examine whether spending aligns with these recommendations.
Specifically, look at:

Whether funded programs are supported by evidence
Whether programs measure outcomes or effectiveness
How officials justify funding decisions

For example, reporting during the investigation examined youth prevention programs funded with opioid settlement dollars and explored whether experts considered those programs evidence-based.

title: Reporting Threads and Investigative Angles
text:
Transparency and oversight
Investigate whether local governments publicly report:

Settlement allocations
Spending decisions
Program outcomes

In some counties, records were difficult to access or inconsistently organized, raising broader questions about transparency and oversight surrounding public health funding.

title: Reporting Threads and Investigative Angles
text:
Differences across jurisdictions
Comparing spending patterns between counties or cities may reveal differences in priorities or approaches. Comparisons can help reporters identify:

Regional spending trends
Uneven access to services
Different interpretations of settlement guidelines

During the West Virginia investigation, some counties prioritized prevention and treatment programs, while others focused funding on law enforcement, administrative costs, or infrastructure projects.

title: Reporting Threads and Investigative Angles
text:
Administrative spending
Some jurisdictions may allocate settlement funds toward administrative costs or enforcement initiatives. Investigating these allocations can reveal:

How governments interpret settlement guidelines
Whether spending aligns with public health recommendations
Whether settlement dollars are being redirected away from direct services

title: Reporting Threads and Investigative Angles
text:
From records to stories
Public records investigations are not only about collecting documents — they are about identifying patterns and connecting records to real-world impact.
The West Virginia investigation produced stories examining:

Youth prevention and education programs
Questions about evidence-based spending
County-level transparency and accountability
Differences in how communities prioritized settlement funding
The challenges of tracking public health dollars across multiple jurisdictions

As records are reviewed, think critically about what the documents reveal, what questions remain unanswered, and how spending decisions affect local communities.

title: Want to know what your local government is spending opioid settlement funds on?
text:
Across the United States, states and local governments are receiving billions of dollars from legal settlements with opioid manufacturers, distributors, and retailers. These settlements stem from lawsuits showing the companies contributed to the opioid epidemic through aggressive marketing, distribution practices, and failure to monitor suspicious orders.
The settlement agreements are expected to distribute more than $50 billion nationally over nearly two decades, with funds flowing to states, counties, cities, and tribal governments.
Many communities hope these funds will support treatment programs, prevention efforts, recovery services, harm reduction initiatives, and other public health responses. However, transparency around how these funds are spent varies widely. In many places, the decision-making process happens at the local level, often with limited reporting requirements or public oversight.
This guide explains how journalists can use public records requests, document analysis, and collaborative reporting methods to track how opioid settlement funds are allocated and spent in their communities.

title: Want to know what your local government is spending opioid settlement funds on?
text:
Why this reporting matters
At the local level:

Local officials determine how funds are spent
Reporting requirements vary or may be minimal
Public documentation of spending decisions is inconsistent

While many states have developed advisory councils or general spending guidelines, there is little consistent oversight over how funds are used at the local level. This lack of standardized transparency creates challenges for journalists and the public trying to understand whether funds are being used for evidence-based solutions — but also creates an opportunity to watchdog how local governments spend a very important pot of money.

title: Want to know what your local government is spending opioid settlement funds on?
text:
What investigating can reveal
Investigating settlement spending can show the gaps between what’s happening and what should happen:

How local governments prioritize prevention, treatment, or enforcement
Whether funds are spent on programs supported by research
Whether spending decisions are made transparently
Whether funds are redirected toward unrelated expenses

Because settlement payments will continue for years, early reporting can help establish accountability and encourage more transparent decision-making going forward.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
section: What counts as a public record?
text:
What counts as a public record?
Generally, records created or maintained by government agencies while conducting official business are considered public records. This may include emails, financial records, meeting minutes, and contracts.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
section: How long does it take to receive records?
text:
How long does it take to receive records?
Response timelines vary by state. Some agencies respond within a few days, while others may take weeks or months, depending on the request scope.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
section: What if agencies don’t have organized records?
text:
What if agencies don’t have organized records?
In some cases, agencies may not maintain clear documentation of spending decisions. This itself may become a reporting finding, highlighting gaps in transparency or recordkeeping.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
section: What if my request is denied?
text:
What if my request is denied?
If an agency denies your request, ask them to cite the specific legal exemption being used. You may be able to:

Narrow the request
Request partially redacted documents
File an appeal under your state’s open records law

title: Frequently Asked Questions
section: What if the municipality or county says they haven’t spent any of the money?
text:
What if the municipality or county says they haven’t spent any of the money?
Then you have a great story. As of March 2026, we are nearly four years into the process of distributing funds. What is keeping the entity from spending them? Is it a lack of knowledge of what to spend it on? Guidance from a state or federal agency? A lack of local resources to plan for spending?
The opportunity is ripe for finding out why they haven’t spent any funds, then asking experts in your community — both medical/academic and people with lived experience — how they should spend it.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
section: My state has funding and a separate process for distributing the funds. What’s the difference between that and the county/municipality?
text:
My state has funding and a separate process for distributing the funds. What’s the difference between that and the county/municipality?
The difference is solely who holds the money and who gets to spend it. Many states, like West Virginia, created state-level nonprofits to distribute state-level funds or gave the responsibility to a specific state entity (like a department, agency, or office).
Those funds come from the same sources, but typically state entities have more resources to determine where, how, and how much to spend. Many municipalities and counties — particularly in rural parts of the country — do not have the same bureaucratic infrastructure. That’s why coverage of local funds is:

Critical — the decisions are happening with little public scrutiny
Ripe for deep-dive data reporting — the records are public, the amounts are significant, and the accountability gap is wide

title: Frequently Asked Questions
section: Can I review the West Virginia documents?
text:
Can I review the West Virginia documents?
Yes. All documents from the investigation are available on DocumentCloud. You can find them by searching “West Virginia Opioid Settlement Spending” or visiting the DocumentCloud project page.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
section: I’m a journalism instructor or student newsroom leader who would like to replicate this process. Do you have help for me?
text:
I’m a journalism instructor or student newsroom leader who would like to replicate this process. Do you have help for me?
Yes. We are turning all of our work into a curriculum for college classrooms. It will be fully complete by May 2026, but there are materials available now to begin planning.

title: Explore West Virginia’s Spending Documents and Applications
text: Curious about what you’ll get out of requests for spending documents? The West Virginia investigation collected records from counties, cities, and municipalities across the state — providing a concrete example of what this reporting looks like in practice.

title: Explore West Virginia’s Spending Documents and Applications
text:
What the WV investigation produced
The investigation filed public records requests with every county in West Virginia, asking for documentation of opioid settlement funds received and how those funds were being spent. The documents received varied widely in format, completeness, and organization.
Examples of records received include:

Budget documents outlining settlement allocations
Physical ledgers (scanned)
Receipt forms
Scanned financial ledgers and checks
Meeting minutes discussing settlement spending
Applications from local organizations
Project outlines

title: Explore West Virginia’s Spending Documents and Applications
section: Using WV as a template for your state
text:
Using WV as a template for your state
The WV investigation is a replicable model. Every state that is party to the national opioid settlements is receiving funds, and local governments within those states are making their own spending decisions — often with little public scrutiny.
The records request process, organizational strategies, and reporting angles described in this guide can be adapted for any state or local jurisdiction.
